narration.full_text: Now, let's put our knowledge of HCF and LCM to the test with some real-world problems. We'll explore scenarios where identifying the correct operation is key to finding the solution. Consider a classic problem: two friends, Anil and Sunil, are running on a circular track. Anil completes a round in 12 minutes, while Sunil takes 18 minutes. If they start at the same point and time, when will they meet again at the starting point? To solve this, we need to find the least common multiple of their individual times. The LCM of 12 and 18 is 36. This means they will meet again at the starting point after 36 minutes. Let's look at another type of problem. Suppose a shopkeeper wants to stack books in equal piles. He has 120 math books and 96 science books. What is the maximum number of books he can put in each pile so that each pile has only one type of book and all piles have the same number of books? Here, we're looking for the greatest common divisor, or HCF, of 120 and 96. The HCF of 120 and 96 is 24. So, the shopkeeper can put a maximum of 24 books in each pile. These examples demonstrate how HCF helps with equal division and LCM helps with finding when events will reoccur simultaneously.
